parts.problem_md:
Fig. 9.1 shows a circuit used in a toy car.

![Circuit diagram with cell P, switch Q, LED S, fixed resistor R, variable resistor T and motor U connected in series, forming a complete electrical circuit.](assets/001-circuit-diagram-with-cell-p-switch-q-led-s-fixed.png)

**Fig. 9.1**

(i) The resistance of component **T** is $5 . 4 Ω$. The resistance of component **U** is $3 . 5 Ω$.

Calculate the combined resistance of components T and U.

[1]

(ii) The current in component R is 2.7 A. The current in component T is 2.5 A.

Determine the current in component S and component U.

[2]

(iii) State the name of component S.

[1]
parts.solution_md:
(i)

To calculate the combined resistance of components T and U:

$R_{TU} = 5 . 4 + 3 . 5$

$= 8 . 9 Ω$

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - $8 . 9 Ω$ **[1 mark]**

(ii)

Using Kirchhoff's current law at the junction, the current in component R splits between the branch containing S and the branch containing T and U:

$I_{S} = I_{R} - I_{T} = 2 . 7 - 2 . 5$

I<sub>S</sub> = **0.2 A**

Since T and U are in series, the current in U is the same as the current in T:

I<sub>U</sub> = **2.5 A**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - current in S = 0.2 A **[1 mark]**
> - current in U = 2.5 A **[1 mark]**

(iii)

> **[mark-scheme]**
> - LED / light-emitting diode **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> At a junction in a circuit, the total current flowing in must equal the total current flowing out (Kirchhoff's current law) — use this to find an unknown branch current when you know the others. Components connected in series (like T and U here) always carry the same current.

(iii)

To calculate the cost of using the heater:

- List the known quantities:

- Power, P = 2.0 kW
- Cost per unit, \$0.15 per kWh
- Time, t = 5.5 hours

- Write down the equation:

$\text{total cost} = \text{cost per kWh} \times \text{power} ( \text{kW} ) \times \text{time} ( \text{hours} )$

In cost calculations, keep power in kilowatts and time in hours throughout so your final answer comes out in the correct currency unit without extra conversions.

parts.problem_md:
A teacher wants to connect an electric heater to the mains supply.

The safety label on the heater states that the heater is double-insulated.

What does the teacher know from reading this label?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- Double insulation means an appliance has two layers of insulation, so there is no risk of the outer casing becoming live
- This means the outer casing does not need to be earthed

choices.label: A
choices.text_md: The outer casing of the heater does not need to be earthed.

choices.label: B
choices.text_md: The outer casing of the heater must be earthed.

choices.label: D
choices.text_md: The heater needs two trip switches.

parts.problem_md:
The diagram shows a 12 V battery connected to an ammeter and two $10 Ω$ resistors.

![Circuit diagram with 12 V battery, ammeter in series, and two 10 Ω resistors connected in parallel between the battery terminals.](assets/003-circuit-diagram-with-12-v-battery-ammeter-in-ser.png)

What is the reading on the ammeter?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is C**

- The two 10 Ω resistors are in parallel, so the combined resistance is found using:

$\frac{1}{R} = \frac{1}{10} + \frac{1}{10}$

$R = 5 Ω$

- Current = voltage ÷ resistance

$I = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{12}{5}$

$= 2 . 4 \text{A}$

**A** is incorrect because $0 . 60 \text{A} = \frac{12}{20}$, treating the resistors as if they were in series (total resistance 20 Ω) instead of parallel

**B** is incorrect because $1 . 2 \text{A} = \frac{12}{10}$, using the resistance of only one resistor instead of the combined parallel resistance

**D** is incorrect because $60 \text{A} = \frac{12}{0.2}$, inverting the combined resistance (using 0.2 Ω instead of 5 Ω)

parts.problem_md:
The diagram shows a battery that is connected to three LEDs, **P**, **Q** and **R**.

![Circuit diagram with a battery and three LEDs labelled P, Q and R; Q and R are in parallel on a branch, with P in series on the main loop.](assets/004-circuit-diagram-with-a-battery-and-three-leds-la.png)

Which of the LEDs are lit?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is D**

- For an LED to emit light it must be forward biased, with conventional current flowing from anode to cathode
- In this circuit, all three LEDs (P, Q, and R) are connected in reverse bias, so no current flows through any of them and none are lit

parts.problem_md:
Two $24 Ω$ resistors are connected in series to a 12 V battery.

![Circuit diagram showing a 12 V battery connected in series to two 24 ohm resistors, forming a simple closed loop](assets/005-circuit-diagram-showing-a-12-v-battery-connected.png)

What is the current in **one** of the resistors?
parts.solution_md:
**Final answer:** **The correct answer is A**

- In series, the total resistance is the sum of the individual resistances

$R_{total} = 24 + 24 = 48 Ω$

- The same current flows through both resistors in a series circuit

$I = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{12}{48}$

$= 0 . 25 \text{A}$

**B** is incorrect because $0 . 50 \text{A} = \frac{12}{24}$, using the resistance of only one resistor instead of the total series resistance

**C** is incorrect because $2 . 0 \text{A} = \frac{48}{24}$, an incorrect combination of the values rather than $V \div R$

**D** is incorrect because $4 . 0 \text{A} = \frac{48}{12}$, inverting the equation ($R \div V$ instead of $V \div R$)
